newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown to shadow the mark.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown to shadow the mark.

text.p: Czech National Bank Governor Josef Tosovsky has said that effective Tuesday the central bank would eliminate its fluctation band within which the Czech crown moves against a mark dollar basket.
"Decisive for the rate of the crown will be the relation of the crown to the mark, and so far no exact fluctation band has been set," Tosovsky told a news conference.
No details on how the crown would shadow the German mark were given, and Tosovsky refused to accept questions following his statement, made late Monday.
Currently the crown is fixed daily within a fluctuation band of plus or minus 7.5 percent against central parity with a basket of currencies comprised of the mark and dollar.

"We expect that the government, in a significant way, will supplement the existing package of measures which it approved recently in a way which would contribute to a faster elimination of the external imbalances," Tosovsky said.
The Czech crown has been under heavy downward pressure recently, as speculators took advantage of a bulging current account and foreign trade deficits to challenge the central bank to intervene.
The central bank intervened on several occassions over the past 10 days to buy crowns to support the exchange rate.
Sitting beside Tosovsky at the news conference in the cabinet headquarters, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said he supported the central bank's measure.
"Today the financial markets are playing against us and the fight with them would be very expensive for us," Klaus said.
Analysts have estimated that the central bank has used several billion dollars of its foreign reserves to defend the crown, the last time coming on Monday afternoon.

"This process is happening... unfortunately our political instability and nervousness contributed to that... Foreign capital is losing its faith in us, and we have to convince it of the opposite quickly," Klaus added.

Klaus and his partners in the three party centre-right coalition government agreed last week to make changes in the cabinet amid the economic downturn and poor approval ratings, and have yet to agree on a new composition of the government.
Klaus said the government was prepared to make further budget cuts to restore confidence in the government's fiscal position.
"We cannot abandon the macroeconomic budgetary or fiscal stability on which this government insists and will insist further," Klaus said.

In late April the government launched a package of measures to kick start the economy, including spending cuts and limits on wage growth as well as import curbs on consumer goods in order to help stem the trade deficit.
Klaus appealed for an end to the volatility in the crown's exchange rate.

"Let's seek a new balanced level of our exchange rate on the market. Let's not try to find any big danger in the movement of the exchange rate. Let's expect that it will be in the tens of hellers (cents) not crowns,"
